title: New England Clam Chowder
subtitle: Creamy potato and clam soup
excerpt: The chowder of Massachusetts and Maine: clams, potatoes, and smoked bacon in a rich, creamy broth thickened with the starchy cooking water from the clams and the potatoes themselves. Served in a wide bowl with oyster crackers on the side.

recipe.sourceNotes: New England clam chowder is white (cream-based), which distinguishes it from the red tomato-based Manhattan clam chowder: a distinction so deeply felt that the state of Maine has at various points introduced bills to ban tomatoes from chowder. The dish was recorded in New England cookbooks from the early nineteenth century, though similar chowders were made by French-Canadian and Portuguese fishermen along the coast before that. The word chowder may derive from the French chaudière (cauldron), the pot in which the soup was made by fishermen communally. Traditional recipes use salt pork rather than bacon; the dominant modern version uses smoked streaky bacon. Canned clams are acceptable and make the dish practical year-round; fresh clams steam open in their own juice and the juice is used as the base of the broth.

content.text: Do not boil the soup once the cream is added: hard boiling causes it to curdle and the clams to toughen. If using fresh clams, steam them in a separate pan and strain the juice through a fine cloth to remove grit before adding to the soup. Add the clam meat right at the end; it needs only 2 to 3 minutes or it turns rubbery.

items.preparation: fresh in shells, scrubbed; or 400 g tinned clams drained with juice reserved
peeled and cut into 1.5 cm cubes

content.text: If using fresh clams, steam them in a pan with 200 ml water over high heat for 3 to 4 minutes until they open. Lift out, reserve the steaming liquid (straining through a fine sieve). Remove the clam meat from the shells. Fry the bacon in a large pan until crisp. Remove with a slotted spoon.

Add the butter to the pan. Cook the onion and celery for 5 minutes until soft. Add the flour and stir for 1 minute. Gradually add the milk, then the clam juice (fresh or from the tin), bay leaves, and thyme. Add the potato and simmer for 15 minutes until very tender.

Add the cream and clam meat. Heat gently without boiling for 2 to 3 minutes until the clams are just heated through. Season with salt and pepper; the clam juice is already salty so taste before adding salt. Remove the bay leaves. Ladle into bowls and scatter with the crisp bacon. Serve with oyster crackers or crusty bread.
